{{Short description|Yang–Mills theory in two dimensions with a well-defined measure}}
In mathematical physics, '''two-dimensional Yang–Mills theory''' is the special case of [[Yang–Mills theory]] in which the dimension of spacetime is taken to be two. This special case allows for a rigorously defined '''Yang–Mills measure''', meaning that the (Euclidean) path integral can be interpreted as a [[Measure_(mathematics)|measure]] on the set of connections modulo gauge transformations. This situation contrasts with the four-dimensional case, where a rigorous construction of the theory as a measure is currently unknown. 

An aspect of the subject of particular interest is the [[1/N_expansion|large-N limit]], in which the structure group is taken to be the [[unitary group]] <math>U(N)</math> and then the <math>N</math> tends to infinity limit is taken. The large-N limit of two-dimensional Yang–Mills theory has connections to string theory.

==Background==

Interest in the Yang–Mills measure comes from a statistical mechanical or constructive quantum field theoretic approach to formulating a quantum theory for the Yang–Mills field. A [[gauge field]] is described mathematically by a 1-form <math>A</math> on a principal <math>G</math>-bundle over a manifold <math>M</math> taking values in the [[Lie algebra]] <math>L(G)</math> of the [[Lie group]] <math>G</math>. We assume that the structure group <math>G</math>, which describes the physical symmetries of the gauge field, is a compact Lie group with a bi-invariant metric on the Lie algebra <math>L(G)</math>, and we also assume given a [[Riemannian metric]] on the manifold <math>M</math>. The Yang–Mills action functional is given by

<math display=block> S_{YM}(A)=\frac{1}{2} \int_M \|F^A\|^2\,d\sigma_M </math>

where <math>F^A</math> is the [[curvature]] of the [[connection form]] <math> A</math>, the norm-squared in the integrand comes from the metric on the Lie algebra and the one on the base manifold, and <math> \sigma_M </math> is the Riemannian volume measure on <math>M</math>.

The measure <math>\mu_T</math>  is given formally by
<math display=block>d\mu_T(A)= \frac{1}{Z_T} e^{-S_{YM}(A)/T} DA,</math>
as a normalized [[probability measure]] on the space of all connections on the bundle, with <math>T>0</math> a parameter, and <math>Z_T</math> is a formal [[normalizing constant]]. More precisely, the probability measure is more likely to be meaningful on the space of orbits of connections under [[gauge transformation]]s.

== The Yang–Mills measure for two-dimensional manifolds ==

Study of Yang–Mills theory in two dimensions dates back at least to work of A. A. Migdal in 1975.<ref name="Migdal 1975"/> Some formulas appearing in Migdal's work can, in retrospect, be seen to be connected to the heat kernel on the structure group of the theory. The role of the heat kernel was made more explicit in various works in the late 1970s, culminating in the introduction of the heat kernel action in work of Menotti and Onofri in 1981.<ref name="Menotti Onofri 1981" />

In the continuum theory, the Yang–Mills measure <math>\mu_T</math> was rigorously defined for the case where <math>M ={\mathbb R}^2</math> by  Bruce Driver<ref name="Driver 1989" /> and by [[Leonard Gross]], Christopher King, and [[Ambar Sengupta]].<ref name="GKS 1989"/> For compact manifolds, both oriented and non-oriented, with or without boundary, with specified bundle topology, the Yang–Mills measure was constructed by Sengupta<ref name="Seng S21992"/><ref name="Seng QGTC1992" /><ref name="Seng YMbound1997"/><ref name="Seng GTCS1997"/> In this approach the 2-dimensional Yang–Mills measure is constructed by using a [[Gaussian measure]] on an infinite-dimensional space conditioned to satisfy relations implied by the topologies of the surface and of the bundle. [[Wilson loop]] variables (certain important variables on the space) were defined using [[stochastic differential equations]] and their expected values computed explicitly and found to agree with the results of the heat kernel action. 

Dana S. Fine<ref name="Fine 1990"/><ref name="Fine 1991" /><ref name= "Fine 1996" /> used the formal Yang–Mills [[Functional integration| functional integral]] to compute loop expectation values. Other approaches include that of Klimek and Kondracki<ref name="KlimKon 1987"/> and Ashtekar et al.<ref name="Ashtekar 1997"/> Thierry Lévy<ref name="Levy 2003"/><ref name ="Levy 2010"/> constructed the 2-dimensional Yang–Mills measure in a very general framework, starting with the loop-expectation value formulas and constructing the measure, somewhat analogously to [[Brownian motion]] measure being constructed from [[Markov chain#Transitions|transition probabilities]]. Unlike other works that also aimed to construct the measure from loop expectation values, Lévy's construction makes it possible to consider a very wide family of loop observables.

The  '''discrete Yang–Mills measure''' is a term that has been used for the [[lattice gauge theory]] version of the Yang–Mills measure, especially for compact surfaces. The lattice in this case is a triangulation of the surface. Notable facts<ref name="Levy 2005"/><ref name="BeckSeng 1998"/> are: (i) the discrete Yang–Mills measure can encode the topology of the bundle over the continuum surface even if only the triangulation is used to define the measure; (ii) when two surfaces are sewn along a common boundary loop, the corresponding discrete Yang–Mills measures convolve to yield the measure for the combined surface.

==Wilson loop expectation values in 2 dimensions==

For a [[piecewise]] smooth loop <math>\gamma</math> on the base manifold <math>M</math> and a point <math>u</math> on the fiber in the principal <math>G</math>-bundle <math>P\to M</math> over the base point <math>o\in M</math> of the loop, there is the [[holonomy]] <math>h_{\gamma}(A)</math> of any [[connection (mathematics)|connection]] <math>A</math> on the bundle. For regular loops <math> \gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_n</math>, all based at <math>o</math> and any function <math>\varphi</math> on <math>G^n</math> the function <math>A\mapsto  \varphi\bigl(h_{\gamma_1}(A),\ldots, h_{\gamma_n}(A)\bigr)</math> is called a [[Wilson loop]] variable, of interest mostly when <math>\varphi</math> is a product of traces of the holonomies in representations of the group <math>G</math>. With <math>M</math> being a two-dimensional Riemannian manifold the loop expectation values

<math display=block>\int \varphi\bigl(h_{\gamma_1}(A),\ldots, h_{\gamma_n}(A)\bigr)\,d\mu_T(A)</math>

were  computed in the above-mentioned works.

If <math>M</math> is the plane then
<math display=block>\int \varphi\bigl(h_{\gamma}(A) \bigr)\,d\mu_T(A) =\int_G \varphi(x) Q_{Ta}(x)\,dx,</math>
where <math>Q_t(y)</math> is the [[heat kernel]] on the group <math>G</math>, <math>a</math> is the area enclosed by the loop <math>\gamma</math>, and the integration is with respect to unit-mass [[Haar measure]]. This formula was proved by Driver<ref name="Driver 1989" /> and by Gross et al.<ref name="Driver 1989" /> using the Gaussian measure construction of the Yang–Mills measure on the plane and by defining parallel transport by interpreting the equation of [[parallel transport]] as a [[Stratonovich integral| Stratonovich]] [[stochastic differential equation]].

If <math>M</math> is the 2-sphere then

<math display=block>\int \varphi\bigl(h_{\gamma}(A) \bigr)\,d\mu_T(A) =\frac{1}{Q_{Tc}(e)} \int_G \varphi(x) Q_{Ta}(x)Q_{Tb}(x^{-1})\,dx,</math>

where now <math>b</math> is the area of the region "outside" the loop <math>\gamma</math>, and <math>c</math> is the total area of the sphere. This formula was proved by Sengupta<ref name="Seng S21992"/> using the conditioned Gaussian measure construction of the Yang–Mills measure and the result agrees with what one gets by using the heat kernel action of Menotti and Onofri.<ref name="Menotti Onofri 1981"/>

As an example for higher genus surfaces, if <math>M</math> is a [[torus]], then

<math display=block>\int \varphi\bigl(h_{\gamma}(A) \bigr)\,d\mu_T(A) =\frac{\int_G \varphi(x) Q_{Ta}(x)Q_{Tb}(x^{-1}wzw^{-1}z^{-1})\,dx \,dw \,dz}{\int_G Q_{Tc}(wzw^{-1}z^{-1})\,dw\,dz}, </math>

with <math>c</math> being the total area of the torus, and <math>\gamma</math> a contractible loop on the torus enclosing an area <math>a</math>. This, and counterparts in higher genus as well as for surfaces with boundary and for bundles with nontrivial topology, were proved by Sengupta.<ref name="Seng QGTC1992" /><ref name="Seng GTCS1997"/>

There is an extensive physics literature on loop expectation values in two-dimensional Yang–Mills theory.<ref name="Grossetal 1993"/><ref name="Cordesetal 1997"/><ref name="KazakKos 1980"/><ref name="Mak 1975"/><ref name="MakMig 1980"/><ref name="MakMig 1981"/><ref name="Rus 1995"/><ref name="Rus 1997"/> Many of the above formulas were known in the physics literature from the 1970s, with the results initially expressed in terms of a sum over the characters of the gauge group rather than the heat kernel and with the function <math>\varphi</math> being the trace in some representation of the group. Expressions involving the heat kernel then appeared explicitly in the form of the "heat kernel action" in work of Menotti and Onofri.<ref name="Menotti Onofri 1981"/> The role of the [[convolution]]  property of the heat kernel was used in works of [[Sergio Albeverio]] et al.<ref name="Albeverio 1988"/><ref name="Albeverio 1989"/> in constructing stochastic cosurface processes inspired by Yang–Mills theory and, indirectly, by Makeenko and Migdal<ref name="MakMig 1980"/> in the physics literature.

==The low-T limit==

The  Yang–Mills [[partition function (mathematics)|partition function]] is, formally,

: <math>\int e^{-\frac{1}{T}S_{YM}(A)}\,DA </math>

In the two-dimensional case we can view this as being (proportional to) the denominator that appears in the loop expectation values. Thus, for example, the partition function for the torus would be

<math display=block>\int_{G^2} Q_{TS}(aba^{-1}b^{-1})\,da\,db,</math>

where <math>S</math> is the area of the torus. In two of the most impactful works<ref name="Witten 1991"/><ref name= "Witten 1992"/> in the field, [[Edward Witten]] showed that as <math>T\downarrow 0</math> the partition function yields the volume of the [[moduli space]] of flat connections with respect to a natural volume measure on the moduli space. This volume measure is associated to a natural [[Symplectic manifold|symplectic structure]] on the moduli space when the surface is [[orientability|orientable]], and is the torsion of a certain complex in the case where the surface is not orientable. Witten's discovery has been studied in different ways by several researchers.<ref name="Forman 1993"/><ref name="KingSeng 1994a"/><ref name="KingSeng 1994b"/> Let <math> \mathcal{M}^0_g</math> denote the [[moduli space]] of flat connections   on a trivial bundle, with structure group being a compact connected semi-simple Lie group <math>G</math> whose Lie algebra is equipped with an Ad-invariant metric, over a compact two-dimensional orientable manifold of genus <math> g\geq 2</math>. Witten showed<ref name="Witten 1991"/> that the symplectic volume of this moduli space is given by 

{{Equation box 1
|title=
|indent=:
|equation = <math display=block> \operatorname{vol}_{\overline{\Omega}} \bigl(\mathcal{M}^0_g\bigr) = |Z(G)|\operatorname{vol}(G)^{2g-2} \sum_\alpha \frac{1}{(\dim\alpha)^{2g-2}}</math>
|border
|border colour =#50C878
|background colour = #ECFCF4
}}


where the sum is over all irreducible representations of <math>G</math>. This was proved rigorous by Sengupta<ref name="Seng 2003" /> (see also the works by [[Lisa Jeffrey]] and by Kefeng Liu<ref name="Liu 1996" />). There is a large literature<ref name="JeffWeitRam 2017" /><ref name="JeffWeit 2000" /><ref name="Gold 1984" /><ref name="Hueb YMsing 1996" /><ref name="Hueb 1996" /> on the  symplectic structure on the moduli space of flat connections, and more generally on the moduli space itself, the major early work being that of [[Michael Atiyah]] and [[Raoul Bott]].<ref name="AB 1983" />

Returning to the Yang–Mills measure, Sengupta<ref name="Seng 2003" /> proved that the measure itself converges in a weak sense to a suitably scaled multiple of the symplectic volume measure for orientable surfaces of genus <math>\geq 2</math>. Thierry Lévy and James R. Norris <ref name="LevyNorris 2006" /> established a [[large deviations theory|large deviations principle]] for this convergence, showing that the Yang–Mills measure encodes the Yang–Mills [[Action (physics)|action]] [[functional (mathematics)| functional]] even though this functional does not explicitly appear in the rigorous formulation of the measure.

==The large-''N'' limit==

The [[1/N_expansion|large-''N'' limit]] of gauge theories refers to the behavior of the theory for gauge groups of the form <math>U(N)</math>, <math>SU(N)</math>, <math>O(N)</math>, <math>SO(N)</math>, and other such families, as <math>N</math> goes to <math>\uparrow \infty</math>. There is a large physics literature on this subject, including major early works by  [[Gerardus 't Hooft]]. A key tool in this analysis is the Makeenko–Migdal equation. 

In two dimensions, the Makeenko–Migdal equation takes a special form developed by Kazakov and Kostov. In the large-N limit, the 2-D form of the Makeenko–Migdal equation relates the Wilson loop functional for a complicated curve with multiple crossings to the product of Wilson loop functionals for a pair of simpler curves with at least one less crossing. In the case of the sphere or the plane, it was the proposed that the Makeenko–Migdal equation could (in principle) reduce the computation of Wilson loop functionals for arbitrary curves to the Wilson loop functional for a simple closed curve. 

In dimension 2, some of the major ideas were proposed by [[Isadore Singer|I. M. Singer]],<ref name="Singer 1995"/> who named this limit the master field (a general notion in some areas of [[physics]]). Xu<ref name="Xu 1997"/> studied the large-<math>N</math> limit of 2-dimensional Yang–Mills loop expectation values using ideas from [[random matrix]] theory. Sengupta<ref name="Seng 2008"/> computed the large-''N'' limit of loop expectation values in the plane and commented on the connection with free probability. Confirming one proposal of  Singer,<ref name="Singer 1995"/> Michael Anshelevich and Sengupta<ref name="AnshSeng 2012"/> showed that the large-''N'' limit of the Yang–Mills measure over the plane for the groups <math>U(N)</math> is given by a [[free probability]] theoretic counterpart of the Yang–Mills measure. An extensive study of the master field in the plane was made by Thierry Lévy.<ref name="Levy 2017"/><ref name="LM2010"/> Several major contributions have been made by Bruce K. Driver, Brian C. Hall, and Todd Kemp,<ref name="DHK 2017"/>  Franck Gabriel,<ref name="Gab 2017"/> and Antoine Dahlqvist.<ref name="Dahl 2016"/>  Dahlqvist and Norris<ref name="DahlNorr 2020"/> have constructed the master field on the two-dimensional sphere.

In spacetime dimension larger than 2, there is very little in terms of rigorous mathematical results. [[Sourav Chatterjee]] has proved several results in large-''N'' gauge theory for dimension larger than 2. Chatterjee<ref name="Chatterjee 2016"/> established an explicit formula for the leading term of the free energy of three-dimensional <math> U(N)</math> lattice gauge theory for any N, as the lattice spacing tends to zero. Let <math>  Z(n,\varepsilon ,g) </math> be the partition function of <math> d</math>-dimensional  <math> U (N) </math> lattice gauge theory with coupling strength <math> g </math> in the box with lattice spacing <math> \varepsilon</math> and size being n spacings in each direction. Chatterjee showed that in dimensions d=2 and 3, <math>\log  Z(n,\varepsilon ,g)</math> is
<math display=block>n^d \left( \frac{1}{2}(d-1)N^2\log(g^2\varepsilon^{4-d}) +(d-1)\log\left( \frac{\prod_{j=1}^{N-1}j!} {(2\pi)^{N/2}} \right) +N^2K_d\right)</math>
up to leading order in <math> n</math>, where <math>K_d</math> is a limiting free-energy term. A similar result was also obtained for in dimension 4, for <math>n\to\infty</math>, <math>\varepsilon\to 0</math>, and <math>g\to 0</math> independently.
